lines.text: {venue}. Mostly empty chairs and a bartender drying the same glass twice.
{venue}. Four or five coats at the bar, nobody near the stand. You can hear the ice machine from the door.
{venue}. About half full. Warm beer, damp wool, and a low hum of talk under the mic check.
{venue}. Half the tables taken, most of them locals who look like they come here every week.
{venue}. Standing room by the cigarette machine. Smoke hanging low over the front tables.
{venue}. Packed to the door. You have to crane your neck past two shoulders just to see the stand.
{venue}. Dim lights, sticky floor, and a PA system that hums before anybody plays a note.
They open with '{first_song}'—one of their own—and the clatter at the bar drops off by the second chorus.
They lead with ‘{first_song}’, one of their own. {lead} keeps pulling your eye back to the stand.
They start with ‘{first_song}’, one of their own. You have to listen past the rough edges to find the tune.
Nothing original on the list, starting with '{first_song}', but they play the standards like they own the copyrights.
Straight down the jukebox list, starting with '{first_song}'. Clean enough to keep drinks moving, nothing you haven't heard since '57.
All covers, starting with ‘{first_song}’. Knowing the song makes it easier to hear where they lose it.
It starts with ‘{first_song}’. You let the room settle around the sound.
Competent. Every bar in town has competent. {lead}'s voice was the best of it, and that's not saying much. The band was the worst.
Put {lead} in front of real session players and you have a record. Leave them with this backing band and you'll waste three hours of studio tape.
The rhythm section is dead tight—they could cut a B-side in two takes. Problem is {lead} disappears right behind the mic.
Forget the rough edges for a second. '{standout_song}' has a real hook—the kind a DJ remembers after one spin. Somebody in this act can write.
Sloppy enough to hear the seams. And somehow the room is still with them.
Easy to admire the playing. Harder to picture anybody crossing town just to hear it twice.
Good enough sound, bad posture. Nobody looked at {lead} between songs. Sign them and you're signing a breakup before summer.
Real chops. They know when to hold back and when to lean in. You wouldn't have to babysit them in the studio.
Steady working band. They know their parts and hit their endings, though nothing tonight made you reach for a pen.
Not ready for a microphone, let alone a pressing plant. Give them another year of Tuesday nights and maybe check back.
Hard to place on one set, but you've got enough to know whether you want to hear more.
The sort of draw you could fit around one big table. It's a beginning.
This is the sound of a full room giving a band its attention.
Full tables can flatter an act. I'd count who stayed before I put money on them.
The room was thin, but the ones who stayed were there to listen.
The chairs tell you how much work there is to do.
A room can like you for a night without going out to buy a 45.
The room took them in stride. Whether that turns into buyers at a counter is another question.
{act} unplug and step off the stand; {lead} does the talking for them. Down at the far end of the bar, {npc} is nursing a glass and watching the door.
The set wraps and {lead} heads for the coats. Near the back booth, {npc} catches your eye and lifts a chin.
{act} come off the stand. Across the room, a guy from {rival_label} is already folding his notebook and standing up.
{act} come off the stand and start coiling cords. {lead} does the talking for them.
The house radio clicks back on while {act} pack up. {lead} is wiping sweat off the neck of a {instrument} near the side door.
Catch {lead} before they pack up the {instrument}.
Wave {lead} over as they come off the stand.
Step up to {lead} while the room clears out.
You count twelve bars against your thumb and wait for the turnaround.
You listen for the shuffle and for what they do with the space at the end of a line.
You try the clapping pattern against your knee to see how quickly a child could pick it up.
You listen to the sing-along refrain with half an ear on how much of it fits in one breath.
You leave your pencil still through the cadence. In a quiet room, even that much would carry.
You follow the phrasing through the rubato, waiting to hear where the pulse settles again.
You stop trying to write down the jokes and start marking the beats before the punch lines.
You keep the opening bit in mind. A callback only works if the room still remembers it.
You tap out the train beat on your knee and try to keep the story straight from verse to verse.
You listen past the twang for the line a jukebox crowd could sing back.
You listen from the bass part up, through the nonsense syllables to the top harmony.
You listen for the vowels in the backing parts. That's where a street-corner harmony starts to sound like one voice.
You listen for the melody through the soft backing. That's the part somebody should be able to hum on the way out.
You listen for the swell into the chorus. At supper-club volume, even a little rise ought to count.
You follow the ballad by its verses, keeping track of who left and who got left behind.
You listen to what changes when the tune comes round again and the singer has another verse to fit inside it.
You listen for the answer to the lead line. In gospel the reply can carry as much weight as the call.
You listen for the lift on each pass through the vamp.
You keep the head in mind through the solo so you'll know where they are when the tune comes back.
You listen for the swing underneath the chorus and let the solo take care of itself for a bar.
You listen for the bolero sway under the melody and count how long it takes you to learn the refrain.
You follow the syncopation under the chorus, tapping the pulse with the heel of your shoe.
You keep time on two and four and listen for the riff that belongs on a 45.
You listen for the breaks. In stop time, the way everybody comes back in can tell you plenty.
You count the backbeat against the edge of your notebook.
You listen for a riff short enough to recognize before the singer gets a word in.
You listen for what the singer does over the vamp once the words have come round twice.
You listen to where the voice sits against the beat, and how long a word can hang there.
You listen to the snap at the front of the guitar notes and for the twang that ought to stay with you after the set.
You try to follow the tune through the fast picking. If you can hum it at that speed, there's a side in it.
You leave a space in the notebook for the title hook and see how soon you can fill it in.
You listen for a middle eight that gives a dance-floor chorus somewhere to go when it comes back.
You catch the polka pulse with your heel and listen to how the melody rides over it.
You listen for the push and pull of a conjunto two-step.
You listen to where the breath falls in the phrase. A pause in the right place can carry half the lyric.
You listen for the bridge and how the singer gets back to the title without leaning too hard on it.
The stub of your pencil snaps. Someone beside you hands over a fresh one with the room's name printed down the side.
As chairs scrape back, somebody asks if any of this set is on a 45. You write down the act's name on the back of their receipt.
Ask who actually wrote '{standout_song}'.
Skip {lead}—buy the rest of the band a quiet drink at the back.
Cut across the floor and get to {lead} before {rival_label} does.
